newsitem.title: JAPAN: International donors pledge $16 bln for Thai rescue.
newsitem.headline: International donors pledge $16 bln for Thai rescue.

text.p: The international community came to the rescue of cash-strapped Thailand on Monday, pledging a total of $16 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund and neighbour states.

The offer, including $4 billion apiece from both Japan and the IMF, is the largest loan package to a single country since the IMF and donors led by the United States made nearly $40 billion available to Mexico in 1995.

Thailand -- long one of Southeast Asia's booming "tiger economies" -- had asked for help to plug financial holes created when it floated its baht currency last month after failing to defend it from speculative attacks.

IMF Deputy Managing Director Shigemitsu Sugisaki told a news conference the IMF had estimated that Thailand needed around $14 billion for 1997 and 1998 and that participants had supported the request.
"The meeting proceeded very smoothly and positively. Some $16 billion in financial support was promised, including the proposed IMF contribution of $4 billion," Sugisaki said.

"The measures they have taken and are going to take will send a good, strong signal to the market and the Fund (IMF) management is going to propose a strong package to the highest board for its consideration."
He also said that Malaysia and other Asian countries had taken steps to make sure there was no spillover effect from Thailand's problems.
Traders and analysts in London said the package would be positive because it reassured players that the IMF had learned lessons from the Mexico crisis.
"They have had a well-coordinated joint action which should give investors a nice warm feeling about the whole situation," said Humaira Sheikhh, an analyst at Australia and New Zealand Banking Group.
The United States is not contributing its own funds to the Thai rescue, but Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said in a statement released in Washington that he welcomed the package.
"The United States looks forward to a rapid conclusion of technical discussions between the Thai authorities and the IMF and the presentation of the adjustment programme to the IMF board," he said.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya told the news conference that the loan package would basically be used to shore up Bangkok's foreign reserves.

Japan, which hosted the meeting, pledged to match the IMF's $4 billion, while Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong will each contribute $1 billion. Sugisaki said South Korea and Indonesia would each lend $500 million.
Contributions from China, which is seriously considering joining the package, and funds from the Asian Development Bank and World Bank may provide another $3 billion.

Analysts said that while Japan wanted the IMF to take the formal lead in forging the package, Tokyo had no alternative but to accept a big part of the burden to ease Bangkok's credit crunch and prevent a chain reaction in the region.
"In terms of who has more at stake, it's pretty clear -- Japan has more at stake," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.
Bangkok has unveiled an austerity package to meet IMF demands, raising value-added tax, announcing plans to cut its current account deficit and closing more than half of its financial institutions.
The cabinet approved a broad outline on Monday to cut its 1997/98 budget by $1.6 billion to $2.3 billion and will review details on August 19, a government spokesman in Bangkok said.
Thailand's sharp economic slowdown has reduced its tax revenue and is yielding the nation's first budget deficits in a decade this year and in fiscal 1997/98.
